author: Procopius of Gaza
occasion: Procopius writes to thank an unnamed correspondent for a letter that delighted him, and to urge the recipient not to leave him in silence.
argument: Procopius praises the recipient's letter as bringing a rational springtime and a musical sound in place of swallows. He says he is transported with pleasure and admires its wording, thought, harmony, and author. He compares himself to the Lydians, who, devoted to Dionysus, observed spring only when Dionysus happened to be present among them. Anticipating that the recipient may laugh and call him a sophist, he insists he cannot help admiring what is beautiful, and asks the recipient not to make him represent in writing the grief that comes from silence.

outline.move: Procopius praises the recipient's wonderful letter as a rational spring and a musical sound in place of swallows, and says he is entranced, admiring its wording, thought, harmony, and author.
He compares himself to the Lydians, devoted to Dionysus, who observed spring only when Dionysus happened to be present among them.
He anticipates being mocked as a sophist, defends his admiration of beauty, and asks the recipient not to make him represent in writing the grief of silence.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He compares himself to the Lydians, who, devoted to Dionysus, observed spring only when Dionysus happened to be present among them
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: καί μοι δοκῶ Λυδὸς ἐξαίφνης εἶναι, τὰ Λυδῶν μιμησάμενος, οἳ τῷ ∆ιονύσῳ προσκείμενοι μόνον ἔαρ ἦγον ἡνίκα δὴ καὶ τύχοι παρ' αὐτοῖς ὁ ∆ιόνυσος
_unresolved_facts.fix: He compares himself to a Lydian, having imitated the Lydians, who, devoted to Dionysus, observed spring only when Dionysus happened to be present among them

_unresolved_facts.claim: Anticipating that the recipient may laugh and call him a sophist
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἀλλὰ μὲν ἴσως ταῦτα γελάσεις, ὡς αὐτόχρημα τὸ σοφιστικὸν ἐπανθεῖ αὐτοῖς, καί με τυχὸν ὡς ἐν ὀνείδει καλέσειας σοφιστήν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Anticipating that the recipient may laugh at these things, as the sophistic element blooms in them in full measure, and perhaps call him a sophist as a reproach

_unresolved_facts.claim: He anticipates being mocked as a sophist, defends his admiration of beauty, and asks the recipient not to make him represent in writing the grief of silence
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: κἂν σιωπήσῃς, ὦ λῷστε, τἀναντία φθεγγόμεθα
_unresolved_facts.fix: He anticipates that the recipient may laugh at his words and call him a sophist, insists he cannot help admiring what is beautiful even if the recipient remains silent (for they speak opposite things), and asks the recipient not to make him represent in writing the grief of silence
